To cut back on
Restless
Nowadays
I used to live ten minutes from downtown.
Every morning I would leave the house before six.
The square used to be full on Sunday evenings.
The station master would shout the name of every stop.
Ana! I was going through some old photos and I found the one from the office Christmas party. Do you remember those?
Of course I do. I used to dread that party every single year.
You did? I always thought you loved it. You would stay until the very end.
I stayed because I was juggling two teams and I could not say no to anybody. I was a creature of habit, and the habit was saying yes.
Fair enough. Honestly, I have cut back on all of that. I do not even go into the office on Fridays anymore.
Good for you. And do you still run errands on Saturday mornings, the way you used to?
Every Saturday, same order, same streets. It is second nature by now. But I am restless, Ana. I keep thinking about doing what you did.
Then come and see it for yourself. I bump into more people here in one week than I did in a whole year down there.
I did not use to have a single free evening.
Nowadays my whole morning takes twenty minutes.
That is second nature to me now.

I have been thinking about this a lot lately. I used to get up at ten past five, every single day, and after the first year I never needed an alarm, because it had become second nature. I would leave the house before six so that I could beat the traffic, and I would eat breakfast standing up at the office. On Saturdays I used to run errands from nine until two: the bank, the market, the pharmacy, the vet. I was juggling all of it and I honestly thought that was normal. The strange part is that I was not unhappy. I was busy, which is not the same thing, and it took me years to learn the difference. Nowadays my whole morning takes about twenty minutes, and I still cannot quite believe it.

People ask me whether I miss the city, and the honest answer is that I miss exactly one thing. I do not miss the hectic mornings. I do not miss the meetings that used to eat my whole afternoon, and I certainly do not miss the fact that I would spend two hours a day in a car going nowhere. I was stuck in a rut and I did not even know it. What I do miss is bumping into people. In the city you would run into somebody you knew every time you left the building: the guy from the bakery, an old colleague, somebody's cousin. Out here I have to make an effort, and I have had to cut back on my excuses. So I go to the market on Saturday mornings, even when I do not need anything, because that is where everybody is.
